tagline.text: A red-brick lighthouse that has lit the northwestern tip of Luzon for over 130 years

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,500 per person (half day from Laoag)

items.credit: Bernard Pasatiempo Recirdo II / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A Spanish colonial-era lighthouse first lit in 1892 that still guides ships along Luzon's northwest coast today. The red-brick building on its hill, the octagonal white tower, and the South China Sea coastline unfolding below are considered a highlight of any northern Ilocos trip.

Cape Bojeador Lighthouse stands on Vigia de Nagpartian Hill in Burgos, Ilocos Norte, and is often called simply "Burgos Lighthouse" locally. Cape Bojeador marks the northwestern tip of Luzon Island, a point every ship rounding from the South China Sea (West Philippine Sea) into the Luzon Strait must pass. The name "Bojeador" is said to come from the Spanish word for sailing around a headland.
The lighthouse was designed in
by Spanish engineer Magín Pers y Pers, with construction completed by Guillermo Brockman of the Lighthouse Service, and it was first lit on
March 30, 1892
. The tower itself stands only about
tall, but because the hill is so high, its light shines out from about
above sea level. It's considered the highest-elevation lighthouse from the Spanish era still operating in the Philippines.

The red-brick-and-plaster compound has three parts: a courtyard, a pavilion once used as the keeper's quarters, and the octagonal tower, topped by a lantern room capped with a bronze dome. It originally used a first-order Fresnel lens and a kerosene lamp, but after the
Luzon earthquake damaged the lens and rotating mechanism, it now runs on a solar-powered electric light. The Philippine government declared it a National Historical Landmark in
and a National Cultural Treasure in

It's a small site that takes just 30 minutes to an hour to see, but the atmosphere is special — the coastline and wind visible from the hilltop, and the moss-flecked brick walls. Sitting along the route from Laoag up to Pagudpud, it pairs well with Kapurpurawan Rock Formation and the Bangui Windmills for a full-day itinerary, and it's an easy stop for history and photography enthusiasts and families alike.
From the parking lot and souvenir shop to the lighthouse is a paved climb of about
5–10 minutes
. The tower gradually comes into view through the trees along the way — a memorable sight — and a shuttle tricycle is available if walking is difficult.
The brick walls, arched doorways, iron gate, and keeper's quarters remain intact after more than 130 years. The contrast between the weathered brick and the white tower photographs beautifully.

blocks.title: Old lighthouse equipment in the small exhibit room

children.text: One side of the pavilion is set up as an exhibit room showing pieces of the old Fresnel lens, a kerosene lamp, and materials on the lighthouse's history. Whether it's open can vary day to day, so ask the caretaker.
From the lighthouse grounds you can look out over Cape Bojeador's coastline and sea, and even the wind turbines toward Bangui in the distance. The sea is at its bluest on a clear dry-season morning.

Since the hill faces west over the water, you can capture the red sky at sunset together with the lighthouse silhouette. Just be sure to come down before visiting hours end, so allow plenty of time when you arrive.

blocks.title: Pair it with Kapurpurawan Rock Formation

children.text: The white limestone coast of Kapurpurawan, also in Burgos, is about
15–20 minutes
away by car. Touring the lighthouse and the rock formation together is the standard route for a northern Ilocos trip.
Pasuquin, between Laoag and Burgos, is known for its crisp baked biscocho and its sea salt. Stop at a roadside bakery on the way to pick up a snack or a gift.

Travel agencies and drivers in Laoag run this same route as a day trip called the "North Tour." If you're traveling with others, chartering a whole vehicle is much more efficient than public transport.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO) in about
1 hour 10 minutes
. From the airport to Burgos Lighthouse is about
, roughly
1 hour–1 hour 20 minutes
by car.
Partas, Florida, Farinas Trans, and other lines run daily buses to Laoag from Cubao, Pasay, and Sampaloc in Manila. The trip takes about
10–12 hours
, with fares of around
depending on seat class. Buses bound for Pagudpud or Aparri pass through Burgos, so you can also get off directly at the lighthouse turnoff.
From Laoag's town terminal, take a Pagudpud- or Claveria-bound bus or minibus and ask to be let off at the "Burgos Lighthouse crossing." It takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
, for a fare of around
Renting a van or car with a driver in Laoag lets you cover the lighthouse, Kapurpurawan, Bangui, and Pagudpud all in one day. A vehicle runs about
— confirm the route and whether fuel is included beforehand.
By private car from Manila, it's about
10–11 hours
via the NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX and the Manila North Road (Maharlika Highway).

From the main road turnoff to the lighthouse's parking lot, you'll go a short way in along a narrow paved road. Take one of the tricycles waiting at the turnoff, or walk; from the parking lot to the lighthouse itself is about
5–10 minutes
uphill on foot, or you can take a shuttle tricycle (about
one way per person).
Ilocos Norte has a clearly defined dry and rainy season. In the
November–May
dry season, clear skies and vivid sea color make for great lighthouse-and-coast photos.
December–February
in particular brings cool northeast monsoon winds, but it's quite windy on the hilltop, so bring a light jacket.
March–May
sees midday temperatures climb to
, making the largely shadeless hill path quite hot.
June–October
falls under the southwest monsoon and typhoon season, and typhoons crossing northern Luzon are especially frequent in
July–September

, which can cut off coastal roads or make a visit difficult due to wind and rain. If visiting in the rainy season, check the forecast and aim for a morning right after the rain clears. The softer light of early morning or late afternoon is best for viewing the lighthouse.

and may vary depending on local conditions.
There's almost no accommodation right around the lighthouse, so most visitors stay in Laoag or Pagudpud. Laoag town has plenty of hotels and pensions at about
a night, convenient for getting around, while if you'd rather relax by the sea, the beach resorts of Pagudpud (about
a night), about
1 hour
north of the lighthouse, are a good option. A few simple homestays are also available in Burgos town and along its coast.

Ilocos Norte's food is simple but full of flavor. Signature dishes include crispy fried bagnet (pork belly), garlic-forward Laoag longganisa, pinakbet (vegetables stir-fried with bagoong, a fermented fish paste), and Laoag-style orange empanada. Around the lighthouse's souvenir shop there are stalls selling simple drinks and snacks, but proper restaurants are scarce, so plan to eat in Laoag or Pagudpud, or pick up biscocho in advance at a Pasuquin bakery.
Visiting hours are generally daytime only. Official hours often aren't posted, so arrive no later than
4 PM

The tower's interior stairs and lantern room level are frequently closed for preservation and safety reasons. Rather than expecting to climb the tower, focus on the courtyard, exhibit room, and the view.
Admission, donations, and the shuttle fare are all cash only. Bring plenty of small change.
If you're taking the bus, tell the driver or conductor in advance that you're getting off at the "Burgos Lighthouse" crossing — the sign is easy to miss.
The hill path has little shade. Bring a hat, sunscreen, and water, and it's best to avoid the midday sun during the dry season.

The best view of the full lighthouse is from the road below the parking lot, and the best coastline shots are from the edge of the lighthouse grounds. Get permission from the local caretaker before flying a drone.
It's hard to cover several northern sights using public transport alone. For a group of 2–4, chartering a vehicle in Laoag and splitting the cost is the more economical option.
The lighthouse is still a working navigational aid. Don't touch the equipment or exhibits, and follow the caretaker's instructions.
The old brick stairs and floors are worn, uneven, and slippery when wet. Some areas have no railing, so hold children's hands firmly and stay out of any closed-off sections.
As a National Cultural Treasure, writing on the walls or removing bricks is a punishable offense.
The hilltop is windy. Keep a firm grip on your hat and any light belongings.
During the
July–September
typhoon season, coastal roads may be closed or bus service suspended, so check conditions before you set out.
Earthquakes or repair work can change which areas are open, or close the site temporarily. Check Burgos tourism information or the latest notices before visiting.
After sunset, the hill path has little lighting. Come down before it gets dark.
